title: Value types vs reference types
hook: Assignment copies a value or copies a reference. That is the language contract. Where bits live (stack vs heap) is an implementation detail the CLR is free to optimize — GC mechanics are module 14.

sections.heading: Copy the payload or copy the pointer
sections.prose: Value types (`struct`, enum, built-in numerics, `bool`, `decimal`) store their data in the variable. Assigning `point2 = point1` copies fields. Reference types (`class`, arrays, `string`, delegates) store a reference. Assigning `list2 = list1` makes two variables alias one object; `list2.Add` is visible through `list1`. Boxing copies a value type into an `object` wrapper on the heap — an allocation you pay for when you stuff an `int` into `ArrayList` or a non-generic interface. Unboxing extracts it. Language view: boxing is a conversion to `object`/`ValueType`/interface. Runtime view (generations, LOH, stacks of frames) waits for module 14. `string` is a reference type with value-like equality. Passing a struct into a method copies it unless you use `ref` (members module).

snippets.label: Independent structs vs aliased lists
snippets.explanation: Wrong interview line: “structs always live on the stack.” Right: “assignment copies the value; the CLR may store that value on the stack, in a register, or boxed on the heap.”

interviewTakeaways: Value assignment copies data; reference assignment aliases an object.
Boxing is wrapping a value type as a reference (`object` or interface).
Do not equate value type with “stack” in a senior interview; point at module 14 for GC.
commonPitfalls: Mutating a struct you got from a list indexer and expecting the list to change — you mutated a copy.
Boxing in hot loops (non-generic collections, `object` keys) then blaming GC without measuring.
Thinking `string` is a value type because `==` compares content.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS primitives copy; objects alias. C# makes the same split explicit as value vs reference types, including user-defined structs.
